1:2.t: "In the prophets": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "in Isaiah the prophet". Verse 2 quotes Malachi 3:1 and verse 3 Isaiah 40:3.

1:6.t: Locusts were permitted food (Leviticus 11:22). John's clothing of camel's hair and a leather belt recalled Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). See the notes at Matthew 3:4.

1:23.t: "Impure spirit": the KJV's "unclean spirit", a demon.

2:4.t: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stairway.

2:17.t: "To repentance": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

2:26.t: "In the days of Abiathar the high priest": 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Ahimelech, Abiathar's father, as the priest. The Greek can mean "in the passage about Abiathar", or Mark may name the better-known high priest of that era.

3:8.t: Idumea was the region south of Judea, the old land of Edom.

3:16.t: "These are the twelve He appointed": supplied from the sense; the KJV begins the verse "And Simon he surnamed Peter".

3:18.t: "Simon the Zealot": the KJV's "Simon the Canaanite", from the Aramaic qan'an, "zealous", not the land of Canaan. Zealots were nationalists opposed to Rome. See Matthew 10:4.

3:21.t: "His family": the KJV's "his friends"; the Greek means "those belonging to him", here his relatives (compare 3:31).

3:29.t: "Eternal judgment": the KJV's "eternal damnation"; many early manuscripts read "eternal sin". "Damnation" in 1611 meant condemnation or judgment (see Matthew 23:33).

4:21.t: "Basket": the KJV's "bushel", a grain basket. See Matthew 5:15.

4:38.t: "In the stern": the KJV's "in the hinder part of the ship".

5:1.t: "Gadarenes": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "Gerasenes". All the readings refer to the area southeast of the Sea of Galilee. See Matthew 8:28, which tells of two men.

5:9.t: A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers.

5:20.t: The Decapolis ("ten cities"): a region of Greek cities east of the Jordan; see Matthew 4:25.

6:3.t: "The carpenter": Matthew 13:55 has "the carpenter's son". "Judas": the KJV's "Juda".

6:8.t: "Bag": the KJV's "scrip". "Belts": the KJV's "purse"; money was carried in a fold of the belt. See Matthew 10:9-10.

6:14.t: "King Herod": Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great and ruler of Galilee and Perea. He was a tetrarch, ruling part of a divided kingdom, and is called king by courtesy. See Matthew 14:1.

6:20.t: "He did many things": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "he was greatly puzzled".

6:37.t: "Two hundred denarii": the KJV's "two hundred pennyworth", about eight months' wages.

6:48.t: "Shortly before dawn": the KJV's "about the fourth watch of the night", from about three to six in the morning. See Matthew 14:25.

7:3.t: "Give their hands a ceremonial washing": the KJV's "wash their hands oft". The Greek pygme may mean "with the fist" or "up to the wrist", a particular ritual washing.

7:4.t: "And dining couches": the KJV's "and of tables"; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

7:6.t: A quotation of Isaiah 29:13 from the Greek.

7:11.t: "Corban": a Hebrew word for an offering dedicated to God. By declaring property dedicated to God, a son could avoid supporting his parents. See Matthew 15:5.

7:16.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse.

7:19.t: "And so all foods are purged": the KJV's "purging all meats", meaning that the body cleanses itself of food. Many early manuscripts read the Greek as Mark's comment, "In saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean." Compare Acts 10:9-16.

7:26.t: "Syrian Phoenicia": the KJV's "a Syrophenician by nation", the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, then part of the province of Syria.

7:31.t: "Through the region of the Decapolis": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "went through Sidon, down to the Sea of Galilee and into the region of the Decapolis."

8:10.t: Dalmanutha is not otherwise known; Matthew 15:39 has Magdala.

8:15.t: "The yeast of Herod": the influence of Herod Antipas and his party. Matthew 16:6 has "of the Sadducees".

9:3.t: "Than anyone in the world could bleach them": the KJV's "so as no fuller on earth can white them". A fuller cleaned and whitened cloth.

9:23.t: "If you can believe": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "'If You can'?", Jesus repeating the father's words back to him.

9:29.t: "And fasting": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

9:44.t: Some early manuscripts do not have these verses; verse 48 is the same and is in all manuscripts. The words quote Isaiah 66:24.

9:46.t: Some early manuscripts do not have these verses; verse 48 is the same and is in all manuscripts. The words quote Isaiah 66:24.

9:49.t: "And every sacrifice will be salted with salt": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words. Compare Leviticus 2:13.

10:19.t: "You shall not defraud" may sum up the tenth commandment against coveting.

10:21.t: "Take up the cross": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

"Loved him" (Greek egapesen, from agapao): agape is not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good, even an enemy's; the New Testament uses agape for God's love in Christ; see Matthew 5:43-44. Jesus' hard demand comes from love, not rejection.

10:24.t: "For those who trust in riches": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

11:3.t: "At once he will send it here": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "and He will send it back here shortly", Jesus promising to return the colt.

11:10.t: "In the name of the Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words in this verse.

11:13.t: Fig trees put out small early fruit with their leaves in spring; a tree in full leaf with none would bear no crop.

11:26.t: Some early manuscripts do not have this verse. Compare Matthew 6:15.

12:1.t: The parable echoes Isaiah 5:1-7. "A pit for the winepress": the KJV's "a place for the winefat", the vat below the press.

12:15.t: "A denarius": the KJV's "a penny", a silver coin bearing the emperor's portrait and title, a day's pay for a laborer. See Matthew 22:19.

12:29.t: A quotation of Deuteronomy 6:4-5; verse 31 quotes Leviticus 19:18.
"The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Hebrew Shema Yisrael, "Hear, O Israel"): the confession of faith Jews recite every day. Jesus begins with it: love for God flows from knowing who He is.

12:33.t: "With all your soul": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

12:40.t: "Will be punished most severely": the KJV's "shall receive greater damnation".

12:42.t: "Mites ... a quadrans": the KJV's "two mites, which make a farthing". The mite (Greek lepton) was the smallest copper coin; two made a quadrans, a sixty-fourth of a denarius.

13:8.t: "And troubles": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

13:14.t: "Spoken of by Daniel the prophet": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. "The abomination that causes desolation" is a desecration of the temple, from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. See Matthew 24:15.

13:33.t: "And pray": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

13:35.t: Mark names the four watches of the night in the Roman reckoning.

14:3.t: "Pure nard": the KJV's "spikenard", an expensive perfume from a plant grown in India.

14:5.t: "More than three hundred denarii": the KJV's "more than three hundred pence", about a year's wages.

14:51.t: Many think the young man was Mark himself, the writer of this Gospel.

14:68.t: "And the rooster crowed": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

14:70.t: "And your speech shows it": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts do not have these words.

15:1.t: "The whole Sanhedrin": the KJV's "the whole council".

15:16.t: "The Praetorium": the governor's headquarters, the KJV's "the common hall" in Matthew; see Matthew 27:27.

15:21.t: Alexander and Rufus were apparently known to Mark's readers. Compare Romans 16:13.

15:25.t: "Nine in the morning": the KJV's "the third hour". John 19:14 places the trial before Pilate at "about the sixth hour", perhaps counting differently.

15:28.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it. The quotation is Isaiah 53:12 (compare Luke 22:37).

15:33.t: "Noon ... three in the afternoon": the KJV's "the sixth hour ... the ninth hour".

16:9.t: The KJV includes these verses. The two most ancient complete manuscripts end at verse 8, and some others have a shorter ending. Many scholars think verses 9-20 were added early to complete the book, drawing on the other Gospels and Acts; others defend them as original.

1:1.t: "The good news" (Greek euangelion): the KJV's "the gospel". The word was used of royal announcements, such as a victory or the birth of an heir. See Matthew 4:23. Mark's first line serves as the title of his whole book.

1:10.t: "Torn open" (Greek schizo): the same word describes the temple curtain torn in two at Jesus' death (15:38). At the start and end of Jesus' ministry God opens the way between heaven and earth.

1:12.t: "At once" (Greek euthys): the KJV's "straightway" or "immediately". Mark uses this word more than forty times, giving his Gospel its urgent pace.

1:15.t: "Believe" (Greek pisteuo): to trust, rely on, be persuaded of. It is the verb of pistis, faith. To believe the good news is to commit oneself to it.

2:27.t: "The Sabbath was made for man" (Greek anthropos): for humanity. God gave the Sabbath as a gift of rest (Exodus 20:8-11, Deuteronomy 5:12-15), not a burden.

3:5.t: "Anger ... deeply distressed": Mark alone records Jesus' anger here, mixed with grief at their hardened hearts (Greek porosis, a hardening like a callus).

3:17.t: "Boanerges" (Aramaic bene regesh): "sons of thunder", perhaps for their fiery temper (compare Luke 9:54).

4:11.t: "So that, 'they may be ever seeing but never perceiving'": quoting Isaiah 6:9-10. Parables confirm the hardness of those who have already refused to hear. Matthew 13:13 gives the same teaching as "because".

4:39.t: "Quiet! Be still!" (Greek siopa, pephimoso): literally "Be silent! Be muzzled!", the same verb Jesus used to silence the demon in 1:25. He commands the storm as Lord over creation (Psalm 89:9, 107:29).

5:7.t: "Most High God" (Greek theos hypsistos, Hebrew El Elyon): a title often used by non-Israelites for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18-20, Daniel 4:2).

5:30.t: "Power" (Greek dynamis): the KJV's "virtue", which in 1611 meant power or strength. The same word is used for Jesus' miracles, "works of power".

5:34.t: "Healed ... freed from your suffering" (Greek sozo ... hygies): sozo means both "healed" and "saved"; see Matthew 9:22. Jesus restores her body and her place among His people.

5:41.t: "Talitha koum" (Aramaic): the KJV's "Talitha cumi". Mark keeps Jesus' own words in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, and translates them (also 7:34, 14:36, 15:34).

6:50.t: "It is I" (Greek ego eimi): literally "I am". It can be an ordinary "it is me", but on the lips of one walking on the sea it echoes God's name, "I AM" (Exodus 3:14); see Matthew 14:27. "He was about to pass by them" (6:48) echoes God passing by Moses and Elijah to reveal His glory (Exodus 33:19-22, 1 Kings 19:11).

7:34.t: "Ephphatha" (Aramaic): "Be opened!" Mark keeps Jesus' own words in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, and translates them; see 5:41.

8:24.t: The two-stage healing pictures the disciples themselves, who see Jesus only partly at first (8:18, 8:29-33) and need a second touch to see clearly.

8:29.t: "The Christ" (Greek christos): "anointed one", the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, Messiah, the promised King; see Matthew 1:1. Mark's account is shorter than Matthew 16:16-19 and moves straight to Jesus' teaching about His suffering.

8:35.t: "Life ... soul" (Greek psyche): the same word in both verses. To gain everything and lose one's psyche is to lose one's very self. See Matthew 16:25-26.

9:24.t: "Help me overcome my unbelief" (Greek boethei mou te apistia): honest faith mixed with doubt, which Jesus does not reject.

9:43.t: "Hell" (Greek geenna): Gehenna, from the Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had once been burned to Molech; it became the name for the place of final judgment; see Matthew 5:22. "Fire that will never be quenched" (Greek to pyr to asbeston): unquenchable fire.

10:45.t: "Ransom for many": a ransom (Greek lytron) is the price paid to free a slave or prisoner, and "for many" (anti pollon) means "in place of many", echoing the Servant who bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:11-12); see Matthew 20:28. This verse sums up Mark's Gospel: the Son of Man came to serve and to die for others.

12:30.t: "Heart ... soul ... mind ... strength" (Greek kardia, psyche, dianoia, ischys): together they mean the whole person. Deuteronomy 6:5 lists heart, soul and strength; Mark adds mind, drawing out what "heart" means in Hebrew. See Matthew 22:37.

12:44.t: "All she had to live on" (Greek holon ton bion autes): literally "her whole life". She gave what mattered, not what was left over.

13:32.t: "Nor the Son": in His human life Jesus chose not to know the day of His return. Christians have long seen here the reality of His humanity (compare Philippians 2:6-8).

14:36.t: "Abba" (Aramaic): "Father", the word a child used for his father, warm and respectful. Jesus' use of it in prayer was unheard of. Paul says the Spirit enables believers to cry "Abba, Father" too (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6).

14:62.t: "I am" (Greek ego eimi): here Jesus answers plainly, and His words also echo God's name, "I AM" (Exodus 3:14; see Matthew 14:27). He adds Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, claiming the throne beside God. The high priest heard it as blasphemy.

15:34.t: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" (Aramaic): "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?", the opening line of Psalm 22, which moves from forsakenness to trust and ends in praise. Matthew 27:46 gives the first words in Hebrew, "Eli, Eli".

15:37.t: "Breathed His last" (Greek exepneusen): the KJV's "gave up the ghost", literally "breathed out". Compare Matthew 27:50, where His death is described as an act of His own, giving up His spirit.

15:39.t: "The Son of God": the Greek has no article and could be read "a son of God", as a pagan soldier might have meant, but the Gospel presents his words as a confession of who Jesus truly is (see Matthew 27:54). Mark's Gospel begins with "Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (1:1) and reaches its climax when a Gentile soldier says it at the cross.

16:7.t: "And Peter": the angel names Peter, who had disowned Jesus, to assure him he is still included.

16:16.t: "Condemned" (Greek katakrino): the KJV's "damned", which in 1611 meant condemned by a judge. The verdict depends on unbelief; baptism is not mentioned in the second half.
